title: Find K Closest Elements
description: Brute force to optimized: sorting all elements by distance versus binary searching for the contiguous answer window's starting index.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a sorted integer array arr, two integers k and x, return the k closest integers to x in the array, sorted in ascending order. An integer a is closer to x than b if abs(a-x) < abs(b-x), or abs(a-x) equals abs(b-x) and a is smaller than b.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"k closest values in a SORTED array\"","The answer is always a contiguous window of length k within the sorted array; binary search for the window's start"],["A tie-breaking rule favoring smaller values","Bias the binary search comparison to prefer the left side on ties"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Since arr is sorted, the k closest values to x always form a CONTIGUOUS block within the array (never a scattered subset), because the elements immediately outside any candidate window are always at least as far from x as the elements at the window's edges. This means the whole problem reduces to finding where that window of length k should start.

blocks.title: Analogy: Choosing the k Closest Houses on a Street
blocks.text: Picture houses numbered in increasing order along a street, and wanting the k houses closest to a particular address. Because the street is ordered, the closest k houses always form one unbroken stretch, so the real question is just: where does that stretch begin?

blocks.caption: Because arr is sorted, the k closest values always form one contiguous window, reducing the problem to finding its start

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Result: [1, 2, 3, 4], the window of 4 consecutive values closest to 3.
5. How Should We Think?

Before comparing every element's distance to x individually, notice that because the array is sorted and the answer must be a contiguous window, a binary search can directly locate the window's starting index by comparing the distances at its two edges.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the window [lo, lo+k-1] is being considered, extending it left (making lo smaller) trades away arr[lo+k] (the value just past the current window's right edge) for arr[lo-1] (the value just before its left edge).

Observation 2: The window should shift left only if arr[lo-1] is CLOSER (or equal, favoring the smaller value) to x than arr[lo+k] is; otherwise, it should shift right (or stay).

Observation 3: This can be framed as a binary search over the window's start lo, in the range [0, n-k]: at each candidate lo, compare (x - arr[mid]) to (arr[mid+k] - x); if the left edge is farther (meaning x - arr[mid] is larger), the window should move right (lo = mid+1); otherwise, it should move left or stay (hi = mid).

Observation 4: The tie-breaking rule (prefer the smaller value when distances are equal) is naturally satisfied by using a strict ">" comparison, which favors keeping (not discarding) the left/smaller candidate on ties.

This leads to binary searching the window's starting index lo in [0, n-k], comparing (x - arr[mid]) to (arr[mid+k] - x) at each step to decide which direction to shift, converging on the correct window in O(log(n-k)) time.
6. Brute Force Solution
Sort ALL elements by their distance to x (breaking ties by value), take the first k, then sort those k values back into ascending order.
Step by step algorithm

items: Create a list of (value, distance to x) pairs for every element in arr.
Sort this list by distance, breaking ties by value.
Take the first k elements from this sorted list.
Sort those k values back into ascending order for the final answer.

codes.python:
def find_closest_elements_brute(arr, k, x):
    sorted_by_distance = sorted(arr, key=lambda v: (abs(v - x), v))  # sort ALL elements by distance
    closest_k = sorted_by_distance[:k]
    return sorted(closest_k)                                          # re-sort by value

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting by distance directly implements the problem's comparison rule, correctly identifying the k closest values.
This ignores the fact that arr is ALREADY sorted, and pays an extra O(n log n) sorting cost that a binary search on the window could avoid.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), sorting by distance plus re-sorting the k results.
Space: O(n) for the distance-sorted copy.
Limitation: this discards the fact that arr is already sorted; recognizing that the answer is always a contiguous window allows a binary search for the window's start in O(log(n-k)) instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-sorting from scratch wastes the given structure: arr being already sorted guarantees the k closest values form one contiguous block, so there is no need to consider scattered subsets at all.

Framing it as a binary search: instead of searching for x directly, binary search over the WINDOW'S STARTING INDEX lo, using the comparison between the window's two candidate edges (arr[mid], the potential left edge if extended, versus arr[mid+k], the value that would be dropped) to decide whether to shift the window left or right.

The comparison rule: if x - arr[mid] (distance to the potential new left edge) is GREATER than arr[mid+k] - x (distance to the value that would be dropped from the right), extending left is not beneficial, so shift lo right; otherwise, shift (or keep) lo left.

The core idea: binary search directly for the window's start, using an edge-distance comparison instead of comparing every element to x individually.

Binary search lo in [0, n-k]. At each step, compare x - arr[mid] to arr[mid+k] - x; if the former is strictly greater, move lo to mid+1 (shift right); otherwise, move hi to mid (shift left or stay). Return the k elements starting at the final lo.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3

blocks.caption: Binary search the window start using edge-distance comparisons, converging in O(log(n-k))

blocks.text: Why This Works

Because arr is sorted, the k closest values always form one contiguous window, and the comparison between the window's potential new left edge and the value it would drop from the right correctly determines whether shifting left improves (or ties, favoring the smaller value) the total closeness. This lets binary search converge directly on the optimal window start in O(log(n-k)) time, without ever needing to compare every element to x individually.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log(n-k) + k), the binary search plus copying the final k-length window.
Space: O(k) for the output.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Find K Closest Elements is a strong example of recognizing that "closest k values in a sorted array" reduces to "find the correct contiguous window," turning what looks like a distance-comparison problem into a binary search problem.
Common Mistakes

items: Using ">=" instead of ">" in the comparison, which would break the required tie-breaking rule favoring smaller values.
Forgetting that the search range for lo is [0, n-k], not [0, n-1], since the window must have exactly k elements.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "since arr is sorted, the answer is always a contiguous window, so this becomes a binary search for the window's start" up front demonstrates the key insight clearly before coding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "k closest values in a SORTED array", think: the answer is a contiguous window; binary search for its start using edge-distance comparisons.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you solve this if arr were NOT sorted (requiring a different approach, like a heap)?
How would you adapt the tie-breaking rule if it favored the LARGER value instead?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Any "closest k in a sorted structure" problem, reducible to a sliding-window or binary-search-on-window-start technique.
Binary search on the answer, a recurring theme across many array problems with a monotonic underlying structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The distance-sort approach runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space; the binary-search-on-window-start approach runs in O(log(n-k) + k) time and O(k) space, directly exploiting the sorted input.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: binary search on the starting index of a contiguous answer window, exploiting sorted input.
Core Idea: compare the distance of a candidate window's new left edge to the distance of the value it would drop from the right, shifting the window accordingly.
Time: O(n log n) for the distance-sort approach, O(log(n-k) + k) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: in a sorted array, the k closest values to any target always form one contiguous window.
Interview Difficulty: a great example of binary search generalizing beyond direct value lookup, to window-boundary search.
One line memory trick: binary search the window start; shift right only if the left edge is strictly farther than the dropped right edge.
